text: Lesson 5 covered what KQL is and how its pipe syntax differs from SQL. Now you'll put that shape to work with the three operators you'll reach for in nearly every query you write from here forward: where, project, and take, against a real Sentinel table full of sign-in activity.

where keeps only the rows matching a condition. SigninLogs, filtered to the last day with TimeGenerated greater than ago of one day, then filtered again to ResultType not equal to zero, meaning the sign-in failed. Two where clauses stacked like this act as an AND — a row has to pass both to survive, and writing them on separate lines makes each condition easy to read, or to comment out while testing.

SigninLogs has dozens of columns, but you rarely need all of them. project keeps only the ones you list, in the order you list them: when it happened, who signed in, which app, which IP address, and the result code. That's a clean five-column view instead of scrolling through every raw field Azure AD logs for each sign-in attempt.

take caps how many rows come back — here, at most 50. It's important that take returns an arbitrary sample of matching rows, not necessarily the newest or most severe ones. It's a tool for a quick look while you're building a query, not for a reliable top-50 list — that's what summarize and sort by are for, starting next lesson.

Three operators, one habit, and almost every query in this course starts from some version of it. where narrows the rows down to the ones that matter. project narrows the columns down to the ones you'll actually read. take narrows the row count so a quick exploratory query doesn't flood your screen with results.

Next up: summarizing and aggregating. You'll turn a long list of individual sign-in rows into one ranked line per user, using aggregation functions like count and dcount grouped together with the by clause — the tools built for exactly the ranking job take was never meant for.
